q: Tell me about welcome to Omarchy
a: Omarchy is an omakase Linux distribution based on Arch, the tiling window manager Hyprland, and the desktop construction-kit Quickshell. It ships with everything a modern, savvy computer user needs to be productive immediately. From Neovim (btw) to Chromium, Obsidian to LibreOffice, and Hype to Monologue. Hell, even a retro Winamp-style music player is there!

q: Tell me about getting Started
a: Omarchy is installed using an ISO. You can choose between a full-disk install, which takes over the entire drive, or a free-space install, which puts Omarchy in the unallocated space on a drive — that's how you dual boot alongside Windows or another OS (see dual-boot install — note that you'll need to turn off BitLocker in Windows first). Either way, the installation defaults to full encryption, and the full-disk option will wipe the selected drive, so be sure to take a backup before using an existing one!

q: What is use a wired or 2.4ghz keyboard?
a: The full-disk encryption won't allow you to enter the password from a Bluetooth keyboard at startup. Just like you can't use a Bluetooth keyboard to enter the BIOS on a PC. You'll need a keyboard that either uses a 2.4ghz dongle or a cable (which is much nicer for latency anyway!). I personally love the Lofree Flow84!

q: What is installing for another owner?
a: If you're setting up a machine for someone else — a family member, a new employee, a buyer — you shouldn't be answering the personal questions on their behalf. Hit `Ctrl + C` on the very first screen of the installer (the keyboard selection), and Omarchy will offer to prepare the machine for another owner instead. The system installs right away, but all the personal setup — keyboard layout, username, password — is deferred until the machine boots for the first time.

q: What is language?
a: Omarchy speaks 50 languages — the same set as omarchy.org — and English is the default. To switch, open the Omarchy menu and go to _Setup > Language_, or run `omarchy language <code>` in a terminal (`omarchy language list` shows the codes). The menu, desktop, and Omarchy's own notifications change language immediately, and every application you open afterwards follows too. Apps that were already open switch once you restart them.

Superwhisper opens its settings to choose cloud or local processing, and OPR keeps the application updated.

q: What is installing and updating agents?
a: Except for Hermes, these agents use mise's lazy installation: the first launch installs the CLI, and later launches reuse it. mise also checks an installed agent for a new release at most once every four hours, just before it starts or in the background at a shell prompt. q: What is crash diagnosis?
a: Omarchy watches systemd-coredump for process crashes. When something segfaults, you'll get a "Process crashed" notification — click it, and the crash is handed to your default agent along with Omarchy's diagnose-crash skill, which walks the agent through establishing the facts from the core dump and deciding whether the crash is worth reporting upstream. You can also run it by hand against any PID from `coredumpctl list` with `omarchy agent crash <pid>`.

q: What is removing and restoring defaults?
a: _Remove Preinstalls_ has mise skip Omarchy's tool declarations for your user, by adding them to `ignored_config_paths` in `~/.config/mise/miserc.toml`. _Restore Preinstalls_ removes that line again. Tools you declare yourself, in your own config or in a project's `mise.toml`, keep working either way. If you choose a default agent or set up Python after removing the preinstalls, that tool is added to your own config. Both apply only to your user; other users on the machine keep their own choice.

q: What is chinese, Japanese, and Korean?
a: Chinese, Japanese, and Korean share many characters but draw some of them differently, so the same character looks right to one reader and foreign to another. Picking one of these languages under _Setup > Language_, or its input method, sets the matching forms. To choose them yourself, run `omarchy font cjk jp`, `kr`, `sc`, `tc` (Taiwan), or `hk` (Hong Kong) in a terminal; `omarchy font cjk default` goes back to the system's choice, which is Japanese forms.

q: What is changing your passwords?
a: You have two passwords on an encrypted install: the one that unlocks the drive at boot, and the one you log in and `sudo` with. Setup makes them the same. If a change is interrupted, run _Drive Encryption_ again: it asks for the password that unlocks the drive now and finishes the change.

q: What is passing on a machine you've already used?
a: If you're handing your machine over to someone else, you don't have to reinstall it. Run _Setup > Reset Computer_ in the Omarchy menu, type `reset` to confirm, and reboot. That wipes every user account and everything in `/home`, throws away all the packages and system changes you made since installation, and clears the machine's identity — network connections, host keys, and all. What comes back up is the setup wizard from the first boot, ready for its new owner to enter their own name, password, and encryption password.

q: What is passwordless sudo?
a: Sometimes you want `sudo` to stop asking, most often when an AI agent is doing a long stretch of system work for you. _Setup > Security > Passwordless Sudo_ asks how long to allow access: 15 minutes, 1 Hour, 1 Day, or Permanently. A red warning icon appears beside the other menu bar indicators while access is active. Click it or run the command again to turn access off. You can also pass your own number of minutes (from 1 to 1440) with `omarchy-sudo-passwordless 30`, or use `omarchy-sudo-passwordless permanent`.

a: When `authorized_keys` is present, the install sets the keys up as the user's `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`, enables `sshd`, and opens the firewall for it. q: Tell me getting about Started
a: Omarchy is installed using an ISO. You can choose between a full-disk install, which takes over the entire drive, or a free-space install, which puts Omarchy in the unallocated space on a drive — that's how you dual boot alongside Windows or another OS (see dual-boot install — note that you'll need to turn off BitLocker in Windows first). Either way, the installation defaults to full encryption, and the full-disk option will wipe the selected drive, so be sure to take a backup before using an existing one!

The system installs right away, but all the personal setup — keyboard layout, username, password — is deferred until the machine boots for the first time.

q: What is language on this machine?
a: Omarchy speaks 50 languages — the same set as omarchy.org — and English is the default. To switch, open the Omarchy menu and go to _Setup > Language_, or run `omarchy language <code>` in a terminal (`omarchy language list` shows the codes). The menu, desktop, and Omarchy's own notifications change language immediately, and every application you open afterwards follows too. Apps that were already open switch once you restart them.

One more is status only: a remote session lights up red while someone is connected to this machine through gliff.

q: what is dictation?
a: On fresh installs, Superwhisper is the default dictation backend, using cloud processing without offline model downloads. Choose Superwhisper or Voxtype through _Setup > Defaults > Dictation_ in the Omarchy menu. Selecting a backend installs it if needed and makes it the default for dictation. Voxtype loads a base English model that takes up 150MB; change the model with `voxtype setup model` and other settings through `~/.config/voxtype/config.toml`. Superwhisper opens its settings to choose cloud or local processing, and OPR keeps the application updated.

q: What crash diagnosis?
a: Omarchy watches systemd-coredump for process crashes. When something segfaults, you'll get a "Process crashed" notification — click it, and the crash is handed to your default agent along with Omarchy's diagnose-crash skill, which walks the agent through establishing the facts from the core dump and deciding whether the crash is worth reporting upstream. You can also run it by hand against any PID from `coredumpctl list` with `omarchy agent crash <pid>`.

q: What the is Omarchy Skill?
a: Agent skills help AI use specific tools in a specific way, and Omarchy ships with a default skill for tailoring the system. Like tweaking your Hyprland config, adjusting the bar, or even creating a new theme from scratch. It's symlinked into the skill directories for Claude Code (`~/.claude/skills`), Codex (`~/.codex/skills`), Pi (`~/.pi/agent/skills`), Antigravity (`~/.gemini/config/skills`), Hermes (`~/.hermes/skills` and each `~/.hermes/profiles/*/skills`), and the generic `~/.agents/skills` location, so most harnesses pick it up automatically.

q: What is warnng about direct pacman/yay updates?
a: If you're already familiar with Arch, you might be tempted to just run `pacman -Syu` or `yay -Syu` yourself, but if you do that, you'll miss the snapshot, migrations, and configuration updates that Omarchy runs together with new packages. That's why Omarchy will actually stop a direct system upgrade and point you to `omarchy update` instead. (If you really know what you're doing, the guard will tell you how to bypass it for a single transaction.)

q: What is psasing on a machine you've already used?
a: If you're handing your machine over to someone else, you don't have to reinstall it. Run _Setup > Reset Computer_ in the Omarchy menu, type `reset` to confirm, and reboot. That wipes every user account and everything in `/home`, throws away all the packages and system changes you made since installation, and clears the machine's identity — network connections, host keys, and all. What comes back up is the setup wizard from the first boot, ready for its new owner to enter their own name, password, and encryption password.
